title: Leonardo da Vinci
intro: Leonardo finished very few paintings, and they are now spread across five cities. He spent his life moving between patrons in Florence, Milan, Rome and France, often leaving work half done when something more interesting came along.
This thread follows his working life and the paintings it left behind.

chapters.heading: Apprentice
chapters.text: Leonardo trained in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, a sculptor and painter who supplied Florence’s churches and guild halls. Vasari tells the story that after the young Leonardo painted an angel in Verrocchio’s Baptism of Christ, his master gave up painting.

chapters.heading: The Last Supper
chapters.text: He wrote to the Duke of Milan offering himself mainly as a military engineer, mentioning painting near the end. In Milan he painted the Last Supper on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie, in an experimental technique that started flaking within his lifetime. He also turned a hall of the Sforza castle into a forest of painted trees.

chapters.heading: Lady with an Ermine
chapters.text: In Milan he also painted Cecilia Gallerani, the duke’s teenage mistress, holding an ermine. It was bought for a Polish princess around 1800, the Nazis took it, and it came back to Kraków after the war. It is one of only four portraits of women by Leonardo.

chapters.heading: The battle with Michelangelo
chapters.text: Back in Florence, the republic hired Leonardo and the young Michelangelo to paint rival battle scenes on facing walls of the great council hall. Neither finished. Leonardo’s experimental paint ran, and Michelangelo was called away to Rome.

chapters.heading: A drawing the size of a painting
chapters.text: The Burlington House Cartoon, a full-size chalk drawing of the Virgin, Saint Anne and the infants, was never turned into a painting. The National Gallery bought it in 1962 after a public appeal.

chapters.heading: The Mona Lisa
chapters.text: He started the portrait of Lisa del Giocondo in Florence and kept working on it for years, taking it with him to France, where he died in 1519. It became the world’s most famous painting partly because it was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 and missing for two years.

image: The Last Supper Leonardo Da Vinci - High Resolution.jpg

title: Michelangelo
intro: Michelangelo thought of himself as a sculptor, but popes kept making him paint and build. He spent his working life going back and forth between Florence and Rome, and most of what he made is still in those two cities.
This thread follows him between them, plus two pieces that ended up in Paris and London.

chapters.heading: The Pietà
chapters.text: A French cardinal commissioned a marble of Mary holding the dead Christ for his tomb. Michelangelo was in his early twenties. It is the only work he ever signed, on the sash across Mary’s chest.

chapters.heading: David
chapters.text: Back in Florence, he took a tall block of marble that had been started and abandoned decades before and carved David from it. A committee that included Leonardo decided to put it outside the town hall instead of on the cathedral. It stood there until 1873, when it moved into the Accademia. A copy now stands in its place.

chapters.heading: The tomb
chapters.text: Pope Julius II called him to Rome to build a huge freestanding tomb with more than forty statues. Money and politics cut it down over forty years to a wall tomb with Moses at the centre. In 1506, while he was in Rome, the Laocoön was dug up in a vineyard and he was sent to look at it.

chapters.heading: The ceiling
chapters.text: Julius then made him paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, a job he didn’t want. He worked standing on scaffolding, not lying on his back, and it took four years. Raphael was painting rooms for the same pope down the corridor.

chapters.heading: Two slaves
chapters.text: He carved two bound figures for the tomb, then they were dropped from the plan. He gave them away, and they went to France. They are now in the Louvre.
chapters.image: Dying and Rebellious Slaves by Michelangelo (Louvre).jpg

chapters.heading: The Medici rooms
chapters.text: For the Medici he designed a funeral chapel at San Lorenzo, with reclining figures of Night, Day, Dawn and Dusk, and a library with a staircase that seems to pour into the entrance hall. In 1530, after siding with the republic against the Medici, he is thought to have hidden in a small room under the chapel. Drawings on its walls were found in 1975.
chapters.image: Tomb of Lorenzo, Duke of Urbino, New Sacristy (Medici Chapel), San Lorenzo, Florence (2) (48768615417).jpg

chapters.place: Sistine Chapel and St Peter’s, Rome
chapters.heading: Judgment and the dome
chapters.text: He moved to Rome for good in 1534 and painted the Last Judgment on the chapel’s altar wall. In his seventies he took over the building of St Peter’s and designed its dome, and he laid out the square on the Capitoline Hill. He died in Rome in 1564, and his body was taken to Florence to be buried.
chapters.image: Dome of St. Peter's Basilica by Michelangelo (7990081751).jpg

chapters.heading: A copy for London
chapters.text: The Grand Duke of Tuscany gave Queen Victoria a full-size plaster cast of David. It stands in the V&A’s Cast Courts with other copies of famous works. A plaster fig leaf was made for it so it could be covered for royal visits.

title: Caravaggio
intro: Michelangelo Merisi took his name from the town his family came from, east of Milan. In about fifteen years in Rome he changed how European painting handled light, and he did it while getting into court cases, sword fights and, in 1606, a killing.
He spent his last four years as a fugitive. His paintings are now spread across Europe, some still in the chapels they were made for.

chapters.place: Milan and the town of Caravaggio
chapters.heading: Training in Lombardy
chapters.text: Born in Milan in 1571 and raised partly in Caravaggio after plague killed his father. At 13 he was apprenticed to Simone Peterzano, a Milanese painter who said he had trained under Titian. Lombard painters liked plain, closely observed detail, and he took that with him. His Basket of Fruit, painted later in Rome, is in Milan’s Biblioteca Ambrosiana.

chapters.place: San Luigi dei Francesi and Santa Maria del Popolo, Rome
chapters.heading: Fame in two chapels
chapters.text: He arrived in Rome broke and painted fruit and flowers for other artists. His break was the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi in 1600: the Calling of Saint Matthew, with a shaft of light across a tax office. Two more canvases for Santa Maria del Popolo followed. Both churches are free, and the paintings are still where he hung them.
chapters.image: Paintings by Caravaggio at Contarelli Chapel-3.jpg

chapters.heading: A death on the tennis court
chapters.text: In May 1606 a fight near the tennis courts on Via della Pallacorda ended with Caravaggio killing Ranuccio Tomassoni. He was sentenced to death in absentia, which meant anyone could kill him on sight, and he left Rome.
chapters.image: Caravaggio - David with the Head of Goliath - Vienna.jpg

chapters.heading: Sanctuary in Naples
chapters.text: Naples was Spanish-ruled and outside the Pope’s reach. He was in demand at once: the Seven Works of Mercy, painted for a charity’s chapel, still hangs over its altar. The Flagellation of Christ is at Capodimonte.

chapters.place: Valletta, Syracuse, Messina, Palermo and Porto Ercole
chapters.heading: On the run
chapters.text: In Malta he was made a Knight of the Order of St John, then jailed after another fight, escaped, and was expelled. He moved through Sicily painting altarpieces, went back to Naples, and was badly cut in the face outside a tavern. He died in July 1610 at Porto Ercole, on his way to Rome to ask for a pardon. He was 38.

chapters.heading: Where the paintings went
chapters.text: Collectors and dukes moved his easel paintings north. The Death of the Virgin was turned down by the church that ordered it and bought for the Duke of Mantua on Rubens’s advice; it is now in the Louvre. The Taking of Christ was lost for two centuries and turned up in 1990 in a Jesuit house in Dublin.

title: The Dutch Golden Age
intro: In the 1600s a small, newly independent republic became the richest place in Europe, and its merchants wanted pictures of themselves, their houses and their dinners. Rembrandt, Vermeer and Frans Hals painted for that market.
Their work has since scattered from Amsterdam to Berlin, Paris, London, Vienna and Florence, along with a few stories about who owned it.

chapters.heading: A city of merchants
chapters.text: Amsterdam began digging its ring of canals in 1613 to house the traders who were making it rich. The tall, narrow houses along the Herengracht were built for the same people who bought paintings.
chapters.image: Gerrit Adriaensz. Berckheyde - The Bend in the Herengracht in Amsterdam - WGA1920.jpg

chapters.heading: Frans Hals
chapters.text: In Haarlem, Frans Hals painted portraits so fast you can see each brushstroke. Two of his best are in Berlin: a boy singing with a flute, and Malle Babbe, a real Haarlem woman with a tankard and an owl on her shoulder.
chapters.image: Frans Hals Malle Babbe about 1640-1646 Gemäldegalerie Berlin 9387.jpg

chapters.heading: The Night Watch
chapters.text: An Amsterdam militia company paid Rembrandt for a group portrait, and he painted them moving, half in shadow. It got its name later, when its varnish had darkened. In 1715 it was trimmed on all sides to fit a wall in the town hall.

chapters.heading: A girl at a window
chapters.text: Rembrandt’s Girl at a Window leans on a sill so convincingly that a story grew up about it being set in a real window to fool passers-by. It hangs in Dulwich Picture Gallery in south London, which opened in 1817 as England’s first public art gallery.

chapters.heading: Bathsheba
chapters.text: Rembrandt’s Bathsheba was probably modelled by Hendrickje Stoffels, who lived with him without marrying him. The year he painted it, his church summoned her for living in sin.

chapters.heading: Vermeer’s rooms
chapters.text: In Delft, Johannes Vermeer painted slowly, about 35 pictures in all, most of them one or two people in a room lit from the left. The Milkmaid is in the Rijksmuseum. The Glass of Wine, a quiet courtship by a stained-glass window, is in Berlin.

chapters.heading: Late Rembrandt
chapters.text: Rembrandt went bankrupt in 1656 and lost the house where he had made most of his etchings. His late paintings got rougher and thicker. Van Gogh said he would give ten years of his life to sit in front of The Jewish Bride with a crust of bread.

chapters.heading: The painting Vermeer kept
chapters.text: Vermeer never sold The Art of Painting, which shows a painter at work on a model dressed as the muse of history. In 1940 Hitler bought it for the museum he planned in Linz. It is now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

chapters.heading: Rachel Ruysch
chapters.text: The Golden Age outlived Rembrandt. Rachel Ruysch painted flowers and fruit with insects crawling over them, became court painter to a German prince, and sold her pictures for more than Rembrandt’s had fetched.

chapters.heading: The fake Vermeers
chapters.text: After the war Dutch police arrested Han van Meegeren for selling a Vermeer to Hermann Göring. To avoid a treason charge he admitted he had painted it himself, along with several other “Vermeers”, and proved it by painting another under supervision.

image: The Night Watch - Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn.png

title: Mozart
intro: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756 and spent much of his childhood on the road, shown off by his father to courts across Europe. As an adult he went where the opera commissions were, until he settled in Vienna in 1781 and tried to live without a court job.
This route follows him to the rooms where his music was first heard, most of which you can still sit in.

chapters.heading: Playing for the empress
chapters.text: At six, Mozart played for Empress Maria Theresa at Schönbrunn with his sister Nannerl. The family story is that he slipped on the polished floor, was helped up by the young Marie Antoinette, and announced he would marry her.

chapters.heading: Writing down a secret
chapters.text: Allegri’s Miserere was sung only in the Sistine Chapel in Holy Week, and copying it was forbidden. The fourteen-year-old Mozart heard it once and wrote it out from memory that evening. The Pope made him a knight a few months later.
chapters.image: Pope Pius VII in the Sistine Chapel A29940.jpg

chapters.heading: His first big opera
chapters.text: Milan’s court theatre, then inside the Palazzo Reale, commissioned an opera seria from a fourteen-year-old. Mitridate, re di Ponto ran for more than twenty nights. The theatre burned down in 1776, and La Scala was built to replace it.
chapters.image: Veduta di tre quarti del Palazzo Reale di Milano.jpg

chapters.heading: Idomeneo
chapters.text: Munich’s elector commissioned Idomeneo, and it opened in the little rococo Cuvilliés Theatre in the Residenz. A few months later Mozart quarrelled with his employer, the Archbishop of Salzburg, and was shown out of his service with a kick from the archbishop’s steward.

chapters.heading: Ten years in Vienna
chapters.text: In Vienna he lived on concerts, teaching and commissions, and moved house more than a dozen times. The Domgasse apartment, the grandest, is where he wrote The Marriage of Figaro. He died in December 1791 at Rauhensteingasse, two streets away, with the Requiem unfinished.
chapters.tip: The Mozarthaus museum keeps the Domgasse apartment’s rooms. St Stephen’s, where he married and where his funeral service was held, is around the corner.

chapters.heading: The city that loved him most
chapters.text: Figaro was a bigger hit in Prague than in Vienna, and Prague commissioned the next opera. Mozart conducted the premiere of Don Giovanni at the Estates Theatre on 29 October 1787. The theatre still stands and still plays Mozart.

chapters.heading: A city he never saw
chapters.text: Both Figaro and Don Giovanni are set in Seville, a city Mozart never went to. The Barber of Seville, the prequel to Figaro, was written later by Rossini, and Seville still points out balconies from both stories.
chapters.image: Jardines de la plaza de Santa Cruz.jpg

title: Picasso and Cubism
intro: Picasso grew up in Barcelona, made his name in Paris and painted his best-known picture there about a bombing in the Basque Country. Cubism, which he worked out with Georges Braque, spread from a few studios in Paris to buildings in Prague within a few years.
This thread follows him and the style from Barcelona to the painting that now hangs in Madrid.

chapters.heading: A teenager in Barcelona
chapters.text: His family moved to Barcelona when he was 13, and he studied at the art school where his father taught. The Picasso Museum, in five medieval palaces on Carrer de Montcada, has the student work that shows how quickly he mastered academic painting.
chapters.image: 062 Casa Finestres, Museu Picasso, c. Montcada 23 (Barcelona), pati.jpg

chapters.heading: The Bateau-Lavoir
chapters.text: He settled in Paris in 1904 in a run-down building of studios on a Montmartre hillside, nicknamed the Bateau-Lavoir after the laundry boats on the Seine. He painted his rose period pictures there, then the canvases that led to Cubism.

chapters.heading: Les Demoiselles d’Avignon
chapters.text: The painting of five women he made in the Bateau-Lavoir in 1907 is named after Carrer d’Avinyó, a street of brothels in Barcelona’s Gothic Quarter he knew as a teenager. His friends found it shocking. It is now in New York.

chapters.heading: Little cubes
chapters.text: Georges Braque spent the summer of 1908 in L’Estaque, on Marseille’s northern shore, where Cézanne had painted. His landscapes reduced the houses and viaduct to blocks. A critic described them as made of cubes, and the name stuck.
chapters.image: L'Estaque - Chemin de la Nerthe - Viaduc ferroviaire du Marinier.jpg

chapters.heading: Questioned over the Mona Lisa
chapters.text: When the Mona Lisa was stolen in 1911, police looked at Picasso’s circle. His friend Apollinaire was jailed for several days and Picasso was questioned, because both were linked to small Iberian statues that had been stolen from the Louvre earlier. Picasso had bought two of them.

chapters.place: House of the Black Madonna, Prague
chapters.heading: Cubist buildings
chapters.text: Czech architects were almost alone in turning Cubism into buildings. Josef Gočár’s House of the Black Madonna, a department store just off the Old Town Square, has angled window frames and a staircase to match. It now houses a café on the first floor.

chapters.heading: The first collage
chapters.text: In 1912 he glued a piece of oilcloth printed to look like chair caning onto a small still life and framed it with rope. It is often called the first collage in modern art. It is in the Musée Picasso in the Marais, which opened in 1985.

chapters.heading: Guernica
chapters.text: After German planes bombed the Basque town of Guernica in April 1937, Picasso painted a huge black-and-white canvas for the Spanish Republic’s pavilion at the Paris World’s Fair. He refused to let it go to Spain while Franco was in power. It arrived in 1981 and has hung in the Reina Sofía since 1992.

title: Opera houses
intro: Opera started at Italian courts and became a paying public entertainment in Venice in 1637. Over the next three centuries every capital wanted its own opera house, and some of the most famous first nights were disasters.
This thread visits the houses, the premieres and one assassination.

chapters.heading: Opera goes public
chapters.text: The first public opera house, where anyone with a ticket could get in, opened in Venice in 1637. Claudio Monteverdi, who ran the music at St Mark’s, wrote his last operas for the city’s new theatres. He is buried in the Frari.

chapters.heading: San Carlo
chapters.text: The Bourbon king of Naples built the Teatro di San Carlo next to his palace in 1737. It is the oldest opera house still in use. In the early 1800s its manager, Domenico Barbaja, hired Rossini and then Donizetti to write for it.

chapters.heading: La Scala
chapters.text: La Scala opened in 1778 on the site of a demolished church. Verdi’s Nabucco made his name there in 1842, and Puccini’s Madama Butterfly was booed off at its first night in 1904. In the 1950s it was where Maria Callas sang her greatest roles.

chapters.heading: Shot at a masked ball
chapters.text: King Gustav III built Stockholm’s opera house and was shot at a masked ball there in March 1792. He died two weeks later. Verdi turned the story into Un ballo in maschera, though the censors made him move it to Boston.
chapters.image: Kungliga Operan Royal Swedish Opera Stockholm 2016 01.jpg

chapters.heading: An opera starts a revolution
chapters.text: On 25 August 1830 La Monnaie staged La Muette de Portici, about a Neapolitan revolt. During a duet about love of country the audience began to riot, and the unrest in the streets that night grew into the revolution that created Belgium.
chapters.image: 1004 Royal Theatre of La Monnaie in Brussels Photo by Giles Laurent.jpg

chapters.heading: Tristan in three cities
chapters.text: Wagner began Tristan und Isolde as a political exile in Zurich, where he fell for Mathilde Wesendonck. He wrote the second act in a palazzo on Venice’s Grand Canal. It was called unperformable until Ludwig II of Bavaria paid Wagner’s debts and had it staged in Munich in 1865.

chapters.heading: The Palais Garnier
chapters.text: Charles Garnier’s opera house opened in 1875 after fourteen years of building, with a grand staircase meant for being seen on. A water tank under its foundations gave Gaston Leroux the underground lake in The Phantom of the Opera.
chapters.image: Grand Staircase of Palais Garnier, Paris, France.jpg

chapters.heading: Mahler’s house
chapters.text: The Court Opera on the Ringstrasse opened in 1869. Gustav Mahler ran it from 1897 to 1907 and made it the best in Europe. It burned after bombing in March 1945, and its reopening in 1955, the year Austria regained its independence, was a national event.

chapters.heading: A roof to walk on
chapters.text: Oslo’s opera house opened in 2008 on the harbour at Bjørvika. Its sloping white marble roof rises out of the fjord, and anyone can walk up it, ticket or not.
chapters.image: Roof of the Oslo Opera House.jpg

title: Songs of longing
intro: Many European cities have a song form built on missing something: a home, a lover, a country, a self. Most grew in port districts and poor quarters, often among people who had arrived from somewhere else, and most were looked down on before they became national treasures.
This one has no timeline. Start anywhere, and listen before you read.

chapters.heading: Saudade in the old quarters
chapters.text: Fado comes out of 19th-century Lisbon: sailors’ bars, brothels and taverns in Alfama and Mouraria. The word for its mood is saudade, longing for something gone or never had. Amália Rodrigues took it to the world in the 1950s, and UNESCO listed it in 2011.
chapters.tip: Fado houses start late, often after 9 pm. When a fadista sings, the room goes quiet and stays that way.

chapters.heading: Deep song across the river
chapters.text: Triana, across the Guadalquivir from the cathedral, was home to Gitano families, potters and sailors. The oldest flamenco, cante jondo or “deep song”, is about grief, prison and hunger. Niña de los Peines recorded it in the 1910s, when most of it had never been written down.
chapters.tip: Tablaos are shows for visitors. Peñas, members’ clubs that often let in guests, are where locals listen.

chapters.heading: Songs for the people who left
chapters.text: Millions of Neapolitans emigrated to the Americas, and many of the city’s songs were written for them. “Santa Lucia luntana” is sung from a ship pulling out of the bay. “Munasterio ’e Santa Chiara”, from 1945, asks whether it’s true that Naples has been destroyed, after Allied bombs burned the church.

chapters.heading: One song, played everywhere
chapters.text: Rezső Seress wrote “Szomorú vasárnap” in 1933 and played piano most nights at the Kispipa in the old Jewish quarter. Translated as “Gloomy Sunday”, it went around the world, and the press gave it a reputation as cursed. Billie Holiday’s 1941 version is the best known in English.
chapters.image: Akácfa utca a Rákóczi út felől nézve. Fortepan 15309.jpg

chapters.heading: Refugees in the port
chapters.text: After 1922 more than a million Greeks were expelled from Asia Minor, and many ended up in shanty towns around Piraeus. They brought the music of Smyrna’s cafés, and in the port’s hash dens it became rebetiko: bouzouki songs about exile, prison, drugs and love. The Metaxas dictatorship censored it in the 1930s.

chapters.heading: The voice of the old taverns
chapters.text: Maria Tănase sang the songs of Romania’s lăutari, the mostly Roma musicians who played in taverns and at weddings. She was a star from the late 1930s to her death in 1963, and many Romanians still know her songs by heart.

chapters.heading: Songs for the new arrivals
chapters.text: From the 1960s, millions moved from the Anatolian countryside to Istanbul and built houses on its edges overnight. Arabesk, with Turkish folk tunes, Egyptian strings and lyrics about fate and heartbreak, was their music. State radio kept it off the air for years. It sold on cassettes from the wholesale blocks at Unkapanı.

title: Jazz in Europe
intro: Jazz arrived in Europe with American soldiers and touring bands after the First World War, and Black American musicians soon found they were treated better in Paris than at home. Within a generation every city had its own players.
Under communism in Poland it was first banned and then tolerated, which made it sound like freedom.

chapters.heading: Le jazz hot
chapters.text: In the 1920s Black American musicians filled the clubs of Montmartre. Josephine Baker arrived in 1925 with the Revue Nègre and became the biggest star in Paris, dancing at the Folies Bergère.
chapters.image: Josephine Baker, Amerikaans,Franse artieste, in de Folies Bergère tijdens een optreden, SFA001007973.jpg

chapters.heading: Banjo
chapters.text: Claude McKay, a Harlem Renaissance writer, set his 1929 novel Banjo on the Marseille docks, among Black sailors and drifters from Africa, America and the Caribbean who played music for whatever they could get.

chapters.heading: Jazz in Pera
chapters.text: In the years when Constantinople became Istanbul, Russian refugees and visiting bands brought jazz to the nightclubs and hotel ballrooms of Pera, the European quarter above the Golden Horn.

chapters.heading: Ježek
chapters.text: Jaroslav Ježek wrote jazzy songs and dance numbers for Prague’s satirical Liberated Theatre. He was almost blind and composed in a flat painted deep blue to ease his eyes. He left for New York in 1939 and died there in 1942.

chapters.heading: Django
chapters.text: Django Reinhardt, a Romani guitarist who played with two fingers on his fretting hand after a fire, wrote Nuages in occupied Paris in 1940. His style, gypsy jazz, still plays in the bars of the Saint-Ouen flea market.

chapters.heading: Monica Zetterlund
chapters.text: Stockholm had one of Europe’s liveliest jazz scenes, centred on the Nalen hall. Monica Zetterlund sang American standards with Swedish words and in 1964 recorded an album with the pianist Bill Evans.

chapters.heading: Bluesette
chapters.text: Toots Thielemans, born above a café in the Marolles, played harmonica and guitar, and could whistle along with his own guitar lines. His 1962 waltz Bluesette became a jazz standard.

chapters.heading: Americans in Copenhagen
chapters.text: In the 1960s American players like Dexter Gordon and Ben Webster settled in Copenhagen, where they found steady work and less racism. At Jazzhus Montmartre the teenage bassist Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen backed them night after night.

chapters.heading: Polish jazz
chapters.text: In Stalinist Poland jazz was banned and played in private, the “catacomb” years. After 1956 it came into the open. Krzysztof Komeda recorded Astigmatic in Warsaw in 1965, and in Kraków Tomasz Stańko and the violinist Zbigniew Seifert took it further out.

chapters.heading: Garden Party
chapters.text: A group of Reykjavík schoolfriends called Mezzoforte made a jazz-funk instrumental that reached the British top 20 in 1983, the first time many people heard music from Iceland.

title: Punk
intro: Punk started in London in 1976 and spread across Europe within a couple of years: three chords, cheap clubs, home-made records. In most cities it was also about something local, from boredom to the Troubles.
The stops run roughly in the order punk arrived.

chapters.heading: Year zero
chapters.text: Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood’s shop at 430 King’s Road dressed the Sex Pistols. The scene played the 100 Club and the Roxy, and by 1977 the Clash were singing about London itself.

chapters.heading: Forty people
chapters.text: In June 1976 the Sex Pistols played the Lesser Free Trade Hall to a small crowd. Members of Buzzcocks, Joy Division and the Fall were there, or said they were, and Manchester’s bands came out of it.

chapters.heading: Good Vibrations
chapters.text: In Belfast during the Troubles, punk was one of the few scenes Catholic and Protestant kids shared. Terri Hooley’s Good Vibrations record shop put out records by local bands, including the Undertones’ “Teenage Kicks”.

chapters.heading: Ça plane pour moi
chapters.text: Plastic Bertrand’s “Ça plane pour moi” was a Europe-wide hit in 1977, a novelty punk single fronted by a Belgian drummer.

chapters.heading: Zurich burns
chapters.text: Zurich’s punk band Kleenex, later LiLiPUT, were four women whose records came out on Rough Trade in London. In 1980 young people rioted for a cultural centre of their own, and got the Rote Fabrik.

chapters.heading: West Berlin
chapters.text: In walled-in West Berlin, Kreuzberg’s SO36 club was the centre of the punk and post-punk scene. Nina Hagen had come over from the East in 1976.

chapters.heading: Ebba Grön
chapters.text: Ebba Grön came out of a youth centre in the Stockholm suburb of Rågsved. “Staten och kapitalet”, the state and capital, became a protest anthem.

chapters.heading: Rokk í Reykjavík
chapters.text: Iceland’s punk scene was tiny but loud. Purrkur Pillnikk and other bands appear in the 1982 film Rokk í Reykjavík. Jón Gnarr, a teenage punk at the time, became the city’s mayor in 2010.

title: Electronic music
intro: Synthesizers came out of studios in West Berlin, Paris and Munich in the 1970s. By the end of the 1980s their sound had moved into clubs in Manchester and London, and after the Wall fell, Berlin’s empty buildings filled with techno.
Most of the places here are clubs and studios, some of them long gone.

chapters.heading: Tangerine Dream
chapters.text: In walled-in West Berlin, Tangerine Dream made long, slow pieces on synthesizers and sequencers. Albums like Stratosfear, from 1976, laid down a sound later heard in every Berlin club.

chapters.heading: Oxygène
chapters.text: Jean-Michel Jarre recorded Oxygène in a home studio, and it sold millions. He later played giant free concerts, including one on the Place de la Concorde in 1979.

chapters.heading: I Feel Love
chapters.text: In a studio under a Munich tower block, Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte built I Feel Love for Donna Summer almost entirely on a Moog synthesizer. Its pulsing bassline seeded house and techno.

chapters.heading: Belgian electronics
chapters.text: Brussels had Telex, a deadpan synth-pop trio, and then Front 242, who called their harsh, marching sound electronic body music. Both fed straight into techno.

chapters.heading: The Haçienda
chapters.text: New Order put royalties from Blue Monday into a huge club, the Haçienda, in 1982. Hardly anyone danced at first. Then acid house arrived in 1988, along with local records like Voodoo Ray, and the Haçienda became the centre of it. It lost money the whole time and closed in 1997.

chapters.heading: Soul II Soul
chapters.text: Soul II Soul started as a sound system playing Sunday nights at the Africa Centre in Covent Garden. Their slow, heavy Back to Life went to number one in 1989.

chapters.heading: After the Wall
chapters.text: West Berlin DJs had been playing house and techno through the 1980s. When the Wall came down, the empty buildings of East Berlin became clubs, and the Love Parade grew from 150 people in 1989 to over a million. Berghain, in a former power station, opened in 2004.

chapters.heading: French touch
chapters.text: In the 1990s Daft Punk and their peers made filtered, disco-flavoured house that the press called French touch. The Rex Club, a basement on the Grands Boulevards, was its home.

chapters.heading: Levels
chapters.text: Tim Bergling, a young producer from Stockholm who called himself Avicii, became one of the biggest names in the global dance boom with Levels. He died in 2018, and the city’s arena was renamed after him.

chapters.heading: Glue
chapters.text: The Belfast duo Bicep grew up going to Shine, a club night at Queen’s University. Their 2017 track Glue is about missing the raves of the 1990s.

title: Eurovision
intro: The Eurovision Song Contest started in 1956 with seven countries. It has launched a few global careers, started at least one revolution and become the place where Europe argues about itself in three-minute songs.
This thread follows a handful of entries back to the cities that sent them.

chapters.heading: Waterloo
chapters.text: ABBA won in Brighton in April 1974 with Waterloo and became one of the biggest-selling groups ever. Their whole story is in a museum on the island of Djurgården.

chapters.heading: A song as a signal
chapters.text: Portugal’s 1974 entry, E Depois do Adeus, came near the bottom. Three weeks later a radio station played it late on 24 April as the first signal for army officers to start a coup against the dictatorship. The second signal, after midnight, was the banned folk song Grândola, Vila Morena.

chapters.heading: Rise Like a Phoenix
chapters.text: Conchita Wurst, the bearded drag persona of Tom Neuwirth, won for Austria in 2014 with a Bond-style ballad and a speech about tolerance. Vienna hosted the contest the next year.

chapters.heading: Portugal finally wins
chapters.text: After more than fifty years of trying, Portugal won in 2017 with Salvador Sobral’s quiet ballad Amar Pelos Dois, written by his sister. Lisbon hosted the contest in 2018.

chapters.heading: Soldi
chapters.text: Mahmood grew up in Gratosoglio, a high-rise estate on Milan’s southern edge. Soldi, about a father who left, includes a line in Arabic. It came second in 2019.

chapters.heading: Måneskin
chapters.text: Måneskin started as teenagers busking on Via del Corso. They won in 2021 with a glam-rock song, the first Italian win since 1990, and went on to tour the world.
chapters.image: Crowds on Via del Corso on a weekend afternoon November 2024.jpg

chapters.heading: In corpore sano
chapters.text: Serbia won in 2007, and Belgrade hosted the next year. In 2022 Konstrakta, an architect turned performer, sat at a basin washing her hands and sang deadpan about health care and beauty standards. It came fifth.

chapters.heading: Cha Cha Cha
chapters.text: Finland won in 2006 with the monster-masked rock band Lordi. In 2023 Käärijä, in a bolero of bright green sleeves, won the public vote with a song about drinking away the working week, and came second overall. His home town painted a mural of him.
chapters.image: Käärijä Eurovision Song Contest Final 2024 interval act.jpg

title: Fire, flood and earthquake
intro: Cities burn, flood and shake, and some of the ones we visit were shaped by the disaster as much as by any architect. London’s skyline after 1666 and Lisbon’s grid after 1755 were both built on ruins.
The most recent of these is still being dealt with, by steel gates under the sea.

chapters.heading: Rome burns
chapters.text: A fire broke out near the Circus Maximus in July 64 and burned for six days. The story of Nero fiddling while it burned is a later invention, but he did use the cleared land for a vast new palace.

chapters.heading: Vesuvius
chapters.text: In 79 Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and hot gas. The towns lay hidden until the 1700s. Loaves found still in a baker’s oven are in the archaeological museum in Naples.

chapters.place: Pudding Lane and the Monument, London
chapters.heading: The Great Fire
chapters.text: In September 1666 a fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane and burned for four days, destroying most of the medieval City, including St Paul’s Cathedral. Christopher Wren rebuilt St Paul’s and designed the Monument near where the fire began.

chapters.heading: All Saints’ Day
chapters.text: On the morning of 1 November 1755 an earthquake flattened much of Lisbon, then a tsunami came up the river and fires burned for days. Tens of thousands died. The Marquis of Pombal rebuilt the lower town on a grid, with buildings framed to survive the next one. The Carmo Convent was left as a ruin.

chapters.heading: The Seine floods
chapters.text: In January 1910 the Seine rose about eight metres and flooded streets, cellars and Métro tunnels for weeks. Parisians still judge floods by how far up the stone Zouave soldier on the Pont de l’Alma the water reaches.
chapters.image: Crue de la Seine. Rue Surcouf, 7ème arrondissement, Paris, le 28 janvier 1910. PH3201.jpg

chapters.heading: Vesuvius again
chapters.text: In March 1944, with Allied troops already in Naples, Vesuvius erupted for eleven days. Lava swallowed the village of San Sebastiano, and falling ash wrecked dozens of American bombers at a nearby airfield.

chapters.heading: The Arno floods
chapters.text: On 4 November 1966 the Arno burst its banks and filled Florence with mud and fuel oil. Volunteers from around the world, the “mud angels”, came to dig out books and paintings. Cimabue’s crucifix in Santa Croce was among the worst damaged.
chapters.image: National Library manuscripts being washed in Florence after the 1966 flood of the Arno - UNESCO - PHOTO 0000001407 0001 - Restoration.jpg

chapters.heading: The 1977 earthquake
chapters.text: On 4 March 1977 an earthquake killed about 1,500 people, most of them in Bucharest, where interwar apartment blocks along the main boulevards collapsed. Ceaușescu used the damage as a reason for the demolitions that followed.

chapters.heading: High water
chapters.text: The same day the Arno flooded Florence, the highest tide on record flooded Venice. After decades of delay, a line of steel gates on the seabed, called MOSE, began rising to close the lagoon in 2020. St Mark’s Square, the lowest part of the city, still floods most often.
chapters.image: San Marco, Acqua Alta - Venice, Italy - panoramio.jpg

title: Exiles
intro: Europe’s cities have always taken in people who couldn’t go home: poets thrown out by rivals, revolutionaries waiting for their moment, refugees from war. Some places became waiting rooms where people sat for months for a visa or a ship.
This thread follows exiles from Dante to people arriving now.

chapters.heading: Dante
chapters.text: In 1302 Dante was exiled from Florence by a rival faction and sentenced to be burned if he came back. He never returned and wrote the Divine Comedy in exile, putting several of his enemies in hell. He died in Ravenna in 1321.

chapters.heading: Lenin, Joyce and Dada
chapters.text: Neutral Switzerland filled with refugees and draft dodgers in the First World War. On one short street in Zurich’s old town, artists founded Dada at the Cabaret Voltaire while Lenin lived a few doors up. James Joyce was writing Ulysses across town. In April 1917 Lenin left by train for Russia.

chapters.heading: A passport for the stateless
chapters.text: The polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen became the League of Nations’ high commissioner for refugees. In 1922 he created the Nansen passport, a travel document for people who had lost their citizenship, and won the Nobel Peace Prize.

chapters.heading: The exchange
chapters.text: After Greece’s defeat in Anatolia, Greece and Turkey agreed in 1923 to swap their minorities by religion. More than a million Orthodox Christians came to Greece. In Athens they built new districts and named them after the towns they had lost, like Nea Smyrni and Nea Ionia.

chapters.heading: Leaving Vienna
chapters.text: After Germany annexed Austria in March 1938, tens of thousands of Viennese Jews fled, leaving homes and art to be taken. Maria Altmann was one of them. Decades later she won back Klimt’s portrait of her aunt, which had hung in the Belvedere.
chapters.image: Palacio Belvedere, Viena, Austria, 2020-02-01, DD 93-95 HDR.jpg

chapters.heading: Marseille
chapters.text: When France fell, refugees crowded into Marseille looking for visas and ships. The American journalist Varian Fry helped about 2,000 people get out, among them Chagall, Hannah Arendt and André Breton. Anna Seghers turned the waiting into the novel Transit.

chapters.heading: The last port
chapters.text: Neutral Portugal was the way out of Europe for many who made it across Spain. Refugees waited in Lisbon’s cafés for a place on a ship to America, sometimes for months.
chapters.image: Westward view from the south end of Rossio, Lisbon, 2010.jpg

chapters.heading: Brodsky’s winters
chapters.text: The Soviet Union expelled the poet Joseph Brodsky in 1972. He settled in the US but spent most winters in Venice and wrote a short book about it. He is buried on the cemetery island of San Michele.

chapters.heading: Arriving now
chapters.text: The war in Syria sent more than a million people to Europe in 2015 and 2016. One Syrian filmmaker recorded his arrival at Amsterdam Centraal. In Paris, a workshop gives exiled artists space and tools.

title: Plague cities
intro: The Black Death killed about a third of Europe’s people in the 1340s, and plague kept coming back for nearly four hundred years. Cities invented quarantine, built churches to give thanks for surviving, and left monuments that are still there.
The stops run in date order.

chapters.heading: The Decameron
chapters.text: Plague reached Florence in 1348 and killed perhaps half the city. Boccaccio’s Decameron opens with seven young women meeting three young men at Santa Maria Novella and leaving town to tell each other stories while it passes.

chapters.heading: Quarantine
chapters.text: Venice set up the first permanent plague hospital on an island in 1423 and kept ships and goods waiting forty days, quaranta giorni. After the plague of 1630–31 it built Santa Maria della Salute to give thanks.
chapters.image: (Venice) - Santa Maria della Salute - Le due cupole e i due campanili.jpg

chapters.heading: The Betrothed
chapters.text: The plague of 1630 killed about half of Milan. Alessandro Manzoni set the climax of The Betrothed, Italy’s best-known novel, in the city’s lazzaretto, with crowds blaming “anointers” for spreading it.
chapters.image: Dal Re, Marc'Antonio (1697-1766) - Vedute di Milano - Il lazzaretto.jpg

chapters.heading: The Great Plague
chapters.text: London’s last great plague killed about a fifth of the city in 1665. Samuel Pepys recorded it in his diary, and then the Great Fire of 1666.
chapters.image: Monument to the Great Fire of London EC3R 8AH.jpg

chapters.heading: The skulls of Fontanelle
chapters.text: The plague of 1656 killed about half of Naples. Many of the dead ended up in a quarry in the Sanità district, later a cemetery. Neapolitans adopted the skulls there and cared for them in return for favours.

chapters.heading: The last great outbreak
chapters.text: In 1720 a ship carrying plague was let into Marseille’s port, reportedly because the merchants who owned its cargo pushed to skip quarantine. Around half the city died. It was the last major plague outbreak in Western Europe.

image: The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg

title: Jewish quarters
intro: Jews have lived in European cities for more than two thousand years. In many of them, the Jewish quarter was where they were allowed or required to live, and its streets, synagogues and cemeteries are among the oldest parts of town.
This thread goes roughly in the order the communities were founded. It includes the Holocaust, but it starts long before it, and in some cities it does not end with it.

chapters.heading: The oldest community
chapters.text: Rome’s Jewish community is the oldest in Europe. The Arch of Titus shows Roman soldiers carrying the menorah looted from Jerusalem in 70 AD. In 1555 a pope walled Rome’s Jews into a ghetto by the Tiber, which lasted until 1870. On 16 October 1943, the Germans rounded up more than a thousand people there; sixteen came back.
chapters.tip: Restaurants along Via del Portico d’Ottavia serve carciofi alla giudia, whole artichokes fried twice.

chapters.heading: Sepharad
chapters.text: Santa Cruz, now the most photographed quarter of Seville, was its judería. In 1391 riots against the Jews started here and spread across Spain. In 1492 the Jews who had not converted were expelled from the country.

chapters.heading: The first ghetto
chapters.text: In 1516 Venice ordered its Jews to live on a small island by an old foundry, a getto, which was locked at night. The word spread to the rest of Europe. With no room to expand, the buildings grew up to seven storeys, taller than anywhere else in the city.

chapters.heading: A refuge
chapters.text: Jews who had been forced to convert in Spain and Portugal found in Amsterdam a city where they could practise openly. Their Portuguese Synagogue opened in 1675 and is still lit by candles. In 1656 the community expelled one of its own, the philosopher Baruch Spinoza.

chapters.heading: The Old-New Synagogue
chapters.text: The Old-New Synagogue, from around 1270, is the oldest working synagogue in Europe. Legend says the clay Golem of Rabbi Loew lies in its attic. Next door, the Old Jewish Cemetery has graves up to twelve layers deep. Franz Kafka was born at the edge of the quarter.
chapters.image: Old New Synagogue- Jewish Town Hall (Prague).jpg

chapters.heading: Kazimierz
chapters.text: King Casimir founded Kazimierz as a separate town in 1335, and from 1495 Kraków’s Jews lived there. In 1941 the Germans moved them across the river into a ghetto in Podgórze. Since the 1990s Kazimierz has come back to life, with restored synagogues and an annual Jewish Culture Festival.
chapters.image: Wolf Popper Synagogue, Entrance gate, 16 Szeroka street, Kazimierz, Kraków, Poland.jpg

chapters.heading: The largest community in Europe
chapters.text: Before the war, about a third of Warsaw was Jewish. Isaac Bashevis Singer grew up on Krochmalna Street, and Janusz Korczak ran his orphanage nearby. In 1940 the Germans sealed off the ghetto. In April 1943 its last inhabitants rose up, and the Germans burned it street by street.

chapters.heading: Europe’s largest synagogue
chapters.text: The Dohány Street Synagogue, finished in 1859, seats about three thousand. Theodor Herzl, who imagined a Jewish state, was born next door. In 1944 Hungary’s Jews were deported in a few weeks; in Budapest, Raoul Wallenberg and other diplomats saved thousands with protective passes.

chapters.heading: A family’s netsuke
chapters.text: Vienna around 1900 was shaped by Jewish families: bankers, doctors, writers, composers. Edmund de Waal traced one of them, the Ephrussis, through a collection of Japanese netsuke hidden by a maid during the war. The Holocaust memorial on Judenplatz is a library whose books cannot be opened.

chapters.heading: Across the Sound
chapters.text: When word came in 1943 that Denmark’s Jews were to be deported, ordinary Danes hid them and ferried about 7,000 across the water to neutral Sweden in a few weeks. Most of the community survived.

image: Old Jewish Cemetery in Josefov, Prague - 8363.jpg

title: The Atlantic slave trade
intro: For four centuries, European ships carried about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic to forced labour in the Americas. The trade was run from Europe’s ports, and the money built warehouses, banks, town halls and country houses that are still there.
Each city here has started, at different speeds, to say so in public.

chapters.heading: Where it started
chapters.text: Portuguese ships began taking captives from West Africa in the 1440s, and Portugal went on to carry more Africans across the Atlantic than any other country, mostly to Brazil. In the 1500s about one in ten people in Lisbon was Black.
chapters.image: Blue facades of waterfront buildings at Ribeira das Naus in Lisbon, Portugal, 20250604 2033 9639.jpg

chapters.heading: The Dutch West India Company
chapters.text: The Dutch West India Company, founded in 1621, traded in slaves from forts on the Gold Coast to colonies such as Suriname. The Netherlands abolished slavery in 1863, among the last in Western Europe. In 1934 the Surinamese writer Anton de Kom published a history of the colony told from the side of the enslaved.

chapters.heading: Denmark’s islands
chapters.text: Denmark held colonies in the Caribbean, now the US Virgin Islands, and shipped sugar and rum home to warehouses like this one on the harbour. It was the first country to pass a law banning the trade, in 1792, though it took effect only in 1803.

chapters.heading: The capital of the trade
chapters.text: London’s Royal African Company held a monopoly on the English slave trade from the 1670s, and the City financed and insured it. Black Londoners, free and enslaved, lived in the city throughout. The British Museum holds an Akan drum carried to Virginia in the 1700s.

chapters.heading: The biggest slaving port
chapters.text: By the end of the 1700s, Liverpool ships carried most of Britain’s trade in enslaved people. The money is in the street names, the Town Hall and the old Exchange. Since 2007, the International Slavery Museum has stood on the dock where slaving ships were fitted out.

chapters.heading: Tobacco and sugar
chapters.text: Glasgow’s “tobacco lords” grew rich on plantations in Virginia and the Caribbean worked by enslaved people. Their mansions and warehouses are the Merchant City, and streets there are still called Virginia Street and Jamaica Street.

title: Spies
intro: For a century, Europe’s cities were where spies met, traded and sometimes died. Neutral capitals, divided cities and grand hotels were the places to be.
The stops run in date order, from the First World War to a poisoned cup of tea in London.

chapters.heading: A nurse before a firing squad
chapters.text: Edith Cavell, a British nurse running a clinic in occupied Brussels, helped hundreds of Allied soldiers escape to the neutral Netherlands. The Germans shot her in October 1915, and Britain made her a martyr. Historians have since found she was also passing on intelligence.

chapters.heading: Orwell’s war
chapters.text: George Orwell came to Barcelona to fight against Franco. His wife Eileen worked in the office of the party militia he joined, and both were watched by Soviet-backed agents. In 1937 the militia was suppressed, and they escaped Spain just in time.
chapters.image: 13 Edifici Telefònica, av. Portal de l'Àngel - pl. Catalunya (Barcelona).jpg

chapters.heading: The neutral port
chapters.text: Portugal stayed neutral in the Second World War, and Lisbon became the last open door out of Europe. Refugees waited for ships to America, and British and German agents worked the same hotels and cafés.

chapters.heading: The Third Man
chapters.text: Postwar Vienna was split between four occupying powers, with a black market in everything. Graham Greene and Carol Reed made The Third Man there in the ruins, with the chase through the sewers and the meeting on the Prater wheel.

chapters.heading: The front line
chapters.text: Berlin was the Cold War’s listening post. The Americans and British built a station on Teufelsberg, a hill made of wartime rubble, to listen into the East. On the Glienicke Bridge the two sides exchanged captured spies, starting in 1962. After 1989, East Germans could read the files the Stasi had kept on them.

chapters.heading: Radio across the Curtain
chapters.text: Radio Free Europe broadcast news into the Eastern bloc from a building beside the English Garden. Communist services planted agents on its staff, and in 1981 its offices were bombed.

chapters.heading: Between the blocs
chapters.text: Tito’s Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948 and belonged to neither side, which made Belgrade a place where both sides met. The café of the Hotel Moskva was a favourite.
chapters.image: Hotel Moskva and the fountain in Belgrade.jpg

chapters.heading: Reading your own file
chapters.text: Romania’s Securitate had one of the largest informer networks in the bloc. The American anthropologist Katherine Verdery did fieldwork there and later read the files it kept on her, in which she appears as a spy.

chapters.heading: Polonium in Mayfair
chapters.text: Alexander Litvinenko, a former Russian security officer living in London, was poisoned with polonium in November 2006 and died three weeks later. A British inquiry concluded that the Russian state was probably behind it.

title: Queer Europe
intro: For most of the twentieth century, gay men in Europe could be jailed for their relationships, and queer life went on in bars, magazines and private clubs. In 1989 Denmark became the first country to recognise same-sex couples, and in 2015 Ireland voted for same-sex marriage.
This thread follows that change through the places where it happened.

chapters.heading: Weimar Berlin
chapters.text: In the 1920s the streets around Nollendorfplatz were full of gay and lesbian bars, and Magnus Hirschfeld ran an institute that studied sexuality. Christopher Isherwood lodged nearby and wrote the stories that became Cabaret. In May 1933 the Nazis ransacked the institute and burned its books.

chapters.heading: Sent away
chapters.text: Fascist Italy didn’t make homosexuality a crime but sent gay men into internal exile on remote islands. Ettore Scola’s film A Special Day takes place on the day Hitler visited Rome in 1938, when a housewife meets a neighbour about to be deported.

chapters.heading: Der Kreis
chapters.text: Switzerland legalised gay sex between adults in 1942. In Zurich, a club and magazine called Der Kreis held discreet dances and published in three languages, until a police crackdown in the 1960s broke it up.

chapters.heading: Alan Turing
chapters.text: The codebreaker, who worked on one of the first computers at Manchester University, was convicted of gross indecency in 1952 and given hormone treatment. He died two years later. A statue of him sits on a bench in Sackville Gardens, by the gay village.

chapters.heading: Tom of Finland
chapters.text: Touko Laaksonen, a war veteran working in advertising, drew muscular, cheerful gay men in a country where homosexuality was illegal until 1971. As Tom of Finland he became famous abroad long before he was accepted at home.
chapters.image: Statue of Johan Ludvig Runeberg on Esplanadi in Helsinki, Finland.jpg

chapters.heading: Pride
chapters.text: During the 1984 miners’ strike, a group of gay and lesbian activists raised money for a mining village in Wales. They met at Gay’s the Word bookshop. The miners later marched at London Pride.
chapters.image: Gay's the Word, London, Bloomsbury, WC1 b.jpg

chapters.heading: After Franco
chapters.text: Spain decriminalised homosexuality in 1979, a few years after Franco’s death. In the Movida, Madrid’s 1980s pop explosion, Alaska’s A quién le importa became an anthem, and Chueca grew into the city’s gay district.

chapters.heading: The first partnerships
chapters.text: On 1 October 1989 Denmark became the first country to let same-sex couples register their partnership. Eleven couples signed at Copenhagen City Hall that day, including the activists Axel and Eigil Axgil.

chapters.heading: The vote
chapters.text: Gay sex was illegal in Ireland until 1993. Twenty-two years later Ireland became the first country to allow same-sex marriage by popular vote, and crowds watched the result come in at Dublin Castle.
chapters.image: Dublin Castle Upper Castle Yard Panorama 01.jpg

title: Cities under bombs
intro: In the Second World War, bombing cities became a strategy rather than an accident. Warsaw, London, Belfast, Naples and Berlin all spent months or years under air raids, and the ruins shaped how they were rebuilt.
This thread visits cities that were bombed and how they remember it.

chapters.heading: Warsaw
chapters.text: When Germany invaded Poland, its planes and artillery bombarded Warsaw for nearly three weeks. The Royal Castle burned, and the city surrendered on 28 September. The castle was rebuilt in the 1970s.

chapters.heading: The Blitz
chapters.text: From September 1940 to May 1941 German bombers attacked London most nights. People sheltered in Tube stations, and Churchill’s government worked from a basement under Whitehall. In March 1943, 173 people were crushed on the stairs of the Bethnal Green station during an alert.

chapters.heading: The May Blitz
chapters.text: Liverpool’s docks were the main port for supplies from America, and it was the most bombed British city outside London. In the first week of May 1941, St Luke’s Church burned out. It was left roofless as a memorial.
chapters.image: St. Luke's Church "Bombed out Church", Liverpool - geograph.org.uk - 7378089.jpg

chapters.heading: Belfast
chapters.text: Belfast had almost no shelters when German bombers came in April 1941. About 900 people died on Easter Tuesday, the most killed in one night anywhere in the UK outside London.

chapters.heading: Naples
chapters.text: Allied planes bombed Naples, Italy’s main southern port, again and again. Families sheltered in the ancient quarries and water tunnels under the city. Sophia Loren grew up in nearby Pozzuoli during the raids.

chapters.heading: A mistake
chapters.text: In March 1945 the RAF bombed the Gestapo’s headquarters in Copenhagen at the Danish resistance’s request. One plane crashed near a French school, and later planes bombed the fire by mistake. Eighty-six children were killed.

chapters.heading: Rubble
chapters.text: By 1945 bombing and the final battle had left much of Berlin in ruins. The broken tower of the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church was kept as a reminder, next to a new church built in the 1960s. Rossellini filmed the rubble in 1947.

chapters.heading: Belgrade
chapters.text: NATO bombed Yugoslavia for 78 days in 1999 over Kosovo. The army headquarters on Kneza Miloša street was hit and left as a ruin, and US bombs hit the Chinese embassy, killing three people.

title: Uprisings
intro: For forty-five years, people in Central and Eastern Europe kept trying to take their cities back. Most attempts were crushed within days or weeks. Each one was remembered, and in 1989 the anniversaries, the funerals and the songs came back.
Each stop is a place you can still stand in.

chapters.heading: Warsaw rises
chapters.text: On 1 August 1944 the Polish Home Army attacked the German occupiers, hoping to free the city before the Red Army arrived. The Soviets stopped on the far bank of the Vistula and waited. The fighting lasted 63 days. Up to 200,000 civilians died, and the Germans then destroyed most of what was left of the city.
chapters.image: Warsaw Uprising - Soldiers from Parasol on Warecka Street.jpg

chapters.heading: Builders strike in East Berlin
chapters.text: Construction workers on Stalinallee walked off the job over higher work quotas. Within a day hundreds of thousands were protesting across East Germany. Soviet tanks put it down, and dozens were killed.
chapters.image: Bundesarchiv B 145 Bild-F005191-0040, Berlin, Aufstand, sowjetischer Panzer.jpg

chapters.heading: Budapest fights the tanks
chapters.text: A student march on 23 October ended with Stalin’s statue pulled down. Young fighters held the Corvin Passage against Soviet armour, and Prime Minister Imre Nagy announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact. On 4 November the Soviet army came back in force. About 2,500 Hungarians were killed and 200,000 fled the country. Nagy was hanged in 1958.
chapters.image: 1956, Budapest, Üllői út - Ferenc körút, Kilián laktanya.jpg

chapters.heading: Students against the censors
chapters.text: When the authorities closed a production of Mickiewicz’s play Dziady for being anti-Russian, students protested. The crackdown came with an antisemitic campaign that pushed about 13,000 Polish Jews to emigrate.

chapters.heading: The end of the Prague Spring
chapters.text: Alexander Dubček had promised “socialism with a human face”: less censorship, more debate. On the night of 20 August, Warsaw Pact armies invaded. In January 1969 the student Jan Palach set himself on fire at the top of Wenceslas Square in protest. Marta Kubišová’s song “Modlitba pro Martu” became an anthem, and she was banned from performing for twenty years.
chapters.image: 10 Soviet Invasion of Czechoslovakia - Flickr - The Central Intelligence Agency.jpg

chapters.heading: A funeral, thirty-one years late
chapters.text: Hungary’s government agreed to rebury Imre Nagy with honours. About a quarter of a million people filled Heroes’ Square. It was the first sign that 1956 could be spoken about in public.

chapters.heading: The Wall opens
chapters.text: Erich Honecker had already been pushed out. At an evening press conference, a Politburo spokesman said the new travel rules applied “immediately”. Crowds went to the checkpoints, and at Bornholmer Straße the guards gave up and opened the gate.

chapters.heading: The Velvet Revolution
chapters.text: Police beat students on Národní street on 17 November. Within days, Wenceslas Square filled every evening. Václav Havel spoke from the Melantrich balcony, and Marta Kubišová, banned since 1970, stood up there beside him. By the end of December Havel was president.

chapters.heading: Ceaușescu’s last speech
chapters.text: On 21 December Nicolae Ceaușescu addressed a rally from the Central Committee balcony, and the crowd booed him on live television. He fled by helicopter the next day. He and his wife were tried and shot on 25 December. Romania’s was the only revolution of 1989 with heavy bloodshed: more than a thousand people died.
chapters.image: PSL during the Romanian Revolution of 1989.jpg

image: Berlin 1989, Fall der Mauer, Chute du mur 10.jpg

intro: In 1968 protest moved across Europe in months, not years. Students in Warsaw and Paris, workers in France, reformers in Prague and singers in Barcelona had different enemies, but they were watching each other.
The chapters follow the calendar.

chapters.heading: A banned play
chapters.text: The authorities closed a production of Mickiewicz’s Dziady for being anti-Russian. Students protested, police beat them at the university gate, and the government answered with an antisemitic campaign that drove about 13,000 Polish Jews to emigrate.

chapters.heading: Easter riots
chapters.text: After the student leader Rudi Dutschke was shot in Berlin on 11 April, students blamed the Springer press and blockaded its offices across West Germany. In Munich two people died. Schwabing, the student district, had just been the setting of the year’s comedy hit, Zur Sache, Schätzchen.

chapters.heading: Barricades in the Latin Quarter
chapters.text: Police cleared the occupied Sorbonne on 3 May. A week later students built barricades in the Latin Quarter, and by the end of the month around ten million workers were on strike. De Gaulle called an election and won it in June.
chapters.image: Prenez vos désirs pour des réalités - 1968.jpg

chapters.heading: Students against the “red bourgeoisie”
chapters.text: Belgrade students occupied their university for a week, protesting unemployment and the privileges of party officials. Tito went on television and said they were partly right, and the protest ended.

chapters.heading: The tanks arrive
chapters.text: Dubček’s Prague Spring had lifted censorship since January. On the night of 20 August, Warsaw Pact armies invaded. Crowds argued with Soviet soldiers on Wenceslas Square, and Marta Kubišová’s “Modlitba pro Martu” became the song of the occupation.

chapters.heading: The stake
chapters.text: Lluís Llach wrote “L’Estaca” in 1968, a song in Catalan about pulling down a rotten stake together, at a time when Franco’s Spain restricted the language. It became an anthem far from Barcelona; in 1978 a Polish version, “Mury”, was taken up by Solidarity.

chapters.heading: Astral Weeks
chapters.text: Northern Ireland’s civil rights marches began that autumn, and students at Queen’s University founded People’s Democracy. In November Van Morrison released Astral Weeks, an album about the Belfast streets he grew up on, months before the city turned violent.

title: Assassinations
intro: Political killings tend to happen in ordinary places: a theatre, a church during Mass, a shopping street, a car at a red light. Several of the spots are marked, and a few are still just street corners.
Some of these killings changed what happened next, and some changed very little.

chapters.heading: Caesar
chapters.text: On the Ides of March, senators stabbed Julius Caesar at a meeting in the Theatre of Pompey. They meant to save the Republic, but his death led to civil war and to his adopted son Augustus becoming emperor. The site is now a sunken square with a cat shelter.

chapters.heading: The Pazzi conspiracy
chapters.text: During Sunday Mass in April 1478, men hired by the rival Pazzi family stabbed Giuliano de’ Medici to death in the cathedral. His brother Lorenzo escaped into the sacristy, and the city hunted down the conspirators within days.
chapters.image: Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence Cathedral, interior, 223756.jpg

chapters.heading: Mary’s court
chapters.text: In 1566 Mary, Queen of Scots, watched her secretary David Rizzio stabbed in her supper room at Holyrood. The next year her husband, Lord Darnley, was found dead after the house he was staying in blew up. Within months she had lost her throne.

chapters.heading: A masked ball
chapters.text: King Gustav III was shot in the back at a masked ball in the opera house he had built. He had been warned and went anyway. He died two weeks later.
chapters.image: Kungliga Operan Royal Swedish Opera Stockholm 2016 01.jpg

chapters.heading: The regicide
chapters.text: On 1 February 1908 republican gunmen shot King Carlos I and his heir in their open carriage as it turned out of the Praça do Comércio. Portugal’s monarchy lasted two more years.

chapters.place: Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius, Prague
chapters.heading: Heydrich
chapters.text: Czechoslovak parachutists trained in Britain ambushed Reinhard Heydrich, the Nazi governor of Bohemia, on a bend in a Prague street. He died of his wounds. The parachutists died weeks later in the crypt of a church, and the Nazis destroyed the villages of Lidice and Ležáky in revenge.

chapters.heading: Carrero Blanco
chapters.text: Franco’s prime minister and closest ally, Luis Carrero Blanco, was killed when the Basque group ETA set off a bomb under his car as he left Mass. The blast threw the car over a church building.

chapters.heading: Palme and Lindh
chapters.text: Prime Minister Olof Palme was shot dead in 1986 walking home from the cinema without bodyguards. No one was ever convicted. In 2003 the foreign minister, Anna Lindh, was stabbed while shopping in a department store a short walk away.

chapters.heading: Đinđić
chapters.text: Zoran Đinđić, the prime minister who had sent Slobodan Milošević to the war crimes tribunal in The Hague, was shot by a sniper outside the government building. The killers were tied to a paramilitary unit and organised crime.

chapters.heading: Theo van Gogh
chapters.text: The filmmaker Theo van Gogh was shot and stabbed on an Amsterdam street by a man angered by his short film about Islam and women. A steel sculpture called The Scream stands in the nearby Oosterpark.

image: Sacred area in Largo di Torre Argentina 02.jpg

title: Heists
intro: Some of the most famous objects in Europe are famous partly because someone took them. Others are still being argued over, two centuries after they were removed.
The thieves here range from a museum handyman to the Nazi leadership to a gang of pensioners.

chapters.heading: The Parthenon sculptures
chapters.text: Around 1801 agents of Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, cut sculptures from the Parthenon and shipped them to Britain. The British Museum has had them since 1816. The Acropolis Museum in Athens, opened in 2009, has a gallery waiting for them.

chapters.heading: The Mona Lisa
chapters.text: In August 1911 Vincenzo Peruggia, who had worked at the Louvre, walked out with the Mona Lisa under his coat. Crowds came to stare at the empty wall. He was caught two years later trying to sell it in Florence, and the painting came home far more famous than it left.

chapters.heading: The Woman in Gold
chapters.text: The Nazis took Klimt’s gold portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer from her family in 1938, and it hung in Vienna’s Belvedere for decades. Her niece Maria Altmann sued Austria and won it back in 2006.

chapters.heading: Göring’s shopping
chapters.text: During the occupation, art seized from Jewish families in France was sorted at the Jeu de Paume in the Tuileries. Hermann Göring came again and again to choose pieces for himself. A curator, Rose Valland, secretly recorded where everything went, which helped return much of it after the war.
chapters.image: Jeu de Paume, Jardin des Tuileries, Paris 25 May 2017.jpg

chapters.heading: The Scream
chapters.text: On the morning the 1994 Winter Olympics opened, two men climbed a ladder into Oslo’s National Gallery, cut The Scream from the wall and left a note thanking it for the poor security. It was recovered three months later. Another version was stolen from the Munch Museum in 2004.
chapters.image: Edvard Munch, The Scream, 1893, National Gallery, Oslo (1) (35658212823).jpg

chapters.heading: The Bührle robbery
chapters.text: In 2008 three armed men walked into a private museum in Zurich and left with four paintings, including a Cézanne and a Van Gogh. All four were eventually found. The collection now hangs in the Kunsthaus.

chapters.heading: The Spider-Man
chapters.text: A burglar known as the Spider-Man cut through a window of the Paris Museum of Modern Art one night in 2010 and took five paintings, including a Picasso and a Matisse. He was caught, but the paintings have never been found.

chapters.heading: Hatton Garden
chapters.text: Over the Easter weekend of 2015 a gang of men mostly in their sixties and seventies drilled through the wall of a safe-deposit vault in London’s jewellery quarter. They were caught within weeks, partly because they talked about it in their cars.

image: Visitors of Louvre in front of Mona Lisa.jpg

title: Organised crime
intro: Port cities and poor estates have bred gangs everywhere, but some have shaped how their cities are seen: Marseille and heroin, Naples and the Camorra, Belgrade’s gangster-celebrities of the 1990s.
Most of the stories here are told by journalists who paid for it, or by films the cities have mixed feelings about.

chapters.heading: Carbone and Spirito
chapters.text: Paul Carbone and François Spirito ran protection, gambling and prostitution in interwar Marseille, with friends in city politics. Borsalino, with Alain Delon and Jean-Paul Belmondo, is loosely based on them.

chapters.heading: The French Connection
chapters.text: Corsican gangs in Marseille refined heroin and shipped it to New York until the network was broken up in the early 1970s. A judge who went after its successors, Pierre Michel, was shot dead in 1981. Today street gangs fight over drug dealing in the northern estates.

chapters.heading: The Special Unit
chapters.text: In 1973 Glasgow’s Barlinnie Prison opened a unit that gave its most violent long-term prisoners art materials and a say in how it was run. Its best-known inmate, the gangster Jimmy Boyle, came out a sculptor and writer.

chapters.heading: The Magliana gang
chapters.text: The Banda della Magliana, named after a district in the south of Rome, ran much of the city’s drug trade and gambling, and was tied to neo-fascists, the secret services and the Vatican bank scandal.

chapters.heading: The Long Good Friday
chapters.text: In The Long Good Friday Bob Hoskins plays a London gang boss who wants to redevelop the derelict docks as the old East End world falls apart around him. A few years later the docks really were redeveloped.
chapters.image: East Dock. St Katharine Docks, London 02.jpg

chapters.heading: The Camorra
chapters.text: The Camorra shot the young reporter Giancarlo Siani in 1985 for writing about it. In 2006 Roberto Saviano’s book Gomorrah named the clans and their business, from fake couture to toxic waste, and he has lived under police protection since. The Vele towers of Scampia, where the clan wars were fought, are being demolished.

chapters.heading: A bomb at the Uffizi
chapters.text: In May 1993 the Sicilian Mafia set off a car bomb in the narrow street behind the Uffizi, part of a campaign against the Italian state. Five people died, and paintings in the gallery were damaged.

chapters.heading: Belgrade’s lost decade
chapters.text: During the wars and sanctions of the 1990s, smugglers and paramilitaries became rich and famous in Belgrade, appearing in magazines and marrying pop stars. The film The Wounds follows two boys from New Belgrade who want to be them.

chapters.heading: Veronica Guerin
chapters.text: The journalist Veronica Guerin was shot at a red light in 1996 after years of writing about Dublin’s drug gangs. Within months Ireland set up the Criminal Assets Bureau to seize criminals’ money.

title: The Roman Empire
intro: At its height Rome ruled from Scotland to Syria, and it left roads, walls, theatres and towns across Europe that later cities were built on top of. Plenty of it is underground, in basements, under squares and under office buildings.
Rome itself comes first, then the provinces, and finally the people who left when the empire fell apart.

chapters.place: Ara Pacis and the Forum, Rome
chapters.heading: Augustus
chapters.text: Caesar’s adopted son Augustus ended the civil wars, called himself first citizen rather than king, and ruled for forty years. The Senate built him the Altar of Peace, and his statue from his wife’s villa shows him as a young general.

chapters.heading: Londinium
chapters.text: The Romans founded Londinium by a bridge over the Thames around 47. Boudica’s rebels burned it in 60 or 61, leaving a red layer archaeologists still find. A temple to Mithras now sits under an office building, and stretches of the wall survive by Tower Hill.
chapters.image: London Roman Wall - surviving section by Tower Hill gardens full section.jpg

chapters.heading: Pompeii
chapters.text: Pompeii is the best picture we have of an ordinary Roman town: its bakeries, bars, graffiti and election slogans, all frozen by the eruption of 79.

chapters.heading: Emperors from Spain
chapters.text: Itálica, outside Seville, was founded for Roman veterans in 206 BC. Trajan, born there, became the first emperor from outside Italy, and his successor Hadrian came from a family there. Hadrian later rebuilt the Pantheon in Rome.
chapters.image: Anfiteatro de las ruinas romanas de Itálica, Santiponce, Sevilla, España, 2015-12-06, DD 34-45 PAN HDR.JPG

chapters.heading: Olisipo
chapters.text: Roman Lisbon, Olisipo, had a theatre on the hillside below the castle. Its remains were found under houses in the 1790s, after the earthquake.

chapters.heading: Singidunum
chapters.text: Belgrade began as Singidunum, a legion’s fortress on the Danube frontier. One of the city’s main streets still follows the Roman road out of the camp.

chapters.heading: Capital of the West
chapters.text: For about a century Milan was the capital of the western half of the empire. In 313 Constantine and his co-emperor agreed there to tolerate Christianity, and the bishop Ambrose later founded the church where he is buried.

chapters.heading: Constantine
chapters.text: After winning Rome at the Milvian Bridge, Constantine got a triumphal arch beside the Colosseum, decorated partly with reliefs taken from older monuments. He went on to found a new capital at Constantinople.

chapters.heading: After Rome
chapters.text: As the empire collapsed, people from mainland towns fled to the islands of the lagoon. Refugees from Altinum settled Torcello, using stone from the old Roman towns, and their settlements grew into Venice.
chapters.image: Venedig Torcello Basilica di Santa Maria Assunta-4345.jpg

image: Colosseum and Arch of Constantine seen from Palatine.jpg

title: Byzantium
intro: The Roman Empire carried on in the east for a thousand years after Rome fell, ruled from Constantinople. The Byzantines called themselves Romans, and their capital was the richest city in Christendom.
Much of what survives was taken elsewhere. This thread starts in the city and follows the loot.

chapters.heading: Hagia Sophia
chapters.text: Justinian’s Hagia Sophia, finished in 537, had the largest dome in the world for nearly a thousand years. It became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020. Its mosaics are still visible upstairs.

chapters.heading: The walls
chapters.text: Three lines of land walls, built in the 400s, kept Constantinople safe for a thousand years. Most of their six kilometres still stand.

chapters.heading: The Fourth Crusade
chapters.text: In 1204 a crusader army meant for Egypt turned on Constantinople instead, sacked it, and put a Latin emperor on its throne. Venice, which had built the fleet, took a large share of the loot.
chapters.image: The Entry of the Crusaders into Constantinople - 1840 - Eugène Delacroix - Louvre - Inv 3821.jpg

chapters.heading: The loot in Venice
chapters.text: The four bronze horses over St Mark’s came from Constantinople’s Hippodrome, and the porphyry Tetrarchs set into the basilica’s corner were taken from the city too. Venice built its sea empire partly on what it took.
chapters.image: Horses of Basilica San Marco bright.jpg

chapters.heading: The Barberini Ivory
chapters.text: An ivory panel of an emperor on horseback, made in Constantinople in the 500s, passed through a Roman cardinal’s collection to the Louvre.

chapters.heading: The Archangel Michael
chapters.text: The largest Byzantine ivory panel to survive, an archangel holding a sceptre and orb, is in the British Museum.

title: Vikings
intro: For about three centuries, Scandinavians raided, traded and settled from Ireland to the Black Sea. Several of today’s capitals began as their towns or were shaped by them.
The stops follow them from their homelands westward.

chapters.heading: At home
chapters.text: Most Vikings were farmers, and raiding was a summer occupation. Denmark’s National Museum holds much of what survives of daily life, from weapons to jewellery.

chapters.heading: East to Byzantium
chapters.text: Swedish Vikings mostly went east, along the rivers of Russia to Constantinople and Baghdad. Silver coins from the Islamic world turn up in Swedish graves by the tens of thousands.

chapters.place: Museum of the Viking Age, Oslo
chapters.heading: The Oseberg ship
chapters.text: In 834, two women were buried in a ship at Oseberg, south of Oslo, with sledges, a cart and animals. The ship survived in the clay for eleven centuries and is now in Oslo’s Viking museum, which is being rebuilt around it.

chapters.heading: Dyflin
chapters.text: Vikings set up a fortified camp on the Liffey in 841, and it grew into a trading town. In the 1970s Dublin built its civic offices on top of the excavated Viking town at Wood Quay, despite large protests.

chapters.heading: Iceland
chapters.text: Norse settlers reached Iceland around 870. The sagas say the first, Ingólfur Arnarson, threw his high-seat pillars overboard and settled where they washed up: Reykjavík. A longhouse from the period is under a hotel on Aðalstræti.

title: The Habsburgs
intro: For four hundred years one family married and inherited its way into ruling much of Europe, from Spain and the Netherlands to Bohemia and Hungary. Its palaces, crypts and art collections are still among the main sights in half a dozen cities.
The thread follows the family west to east and through to its end in 1918.

chapters.heading: Charles V
chapters.text: Charles V was born in Ghent and came of age in Brussels, ruling the Netherlands, Spain, its American colonies and the Holy Roman Empire. In 1555, worn out, he gave up his thrones in the great hall of the Coudenberg Palace in Brussels. Its remains are under the Place Royale.
chapters.image: Brussels, straatzicht Place Royale met église Saint-Jacques-sur-Coudenberg oeg2043-01020 en standbeeld van Godefroid de Bouillon foto3 2015-06-07 13.53.jpg

chapters.heading: The Spanish branch
chapters.text: Charles’s son Philip II made Madrid the capital of Spain. The Spanish Habsburgs collected the paintings that became the Prado. In Las Meninas, Velázquez painted the court of Philip IV around the king’s young daughter. The line ended in 1700 with Charles II, who had no children.

chapters.heading: Rudolf’s court
